title_original: Tim Walker’s Queeristocracy Holds Court in London
excerpt_original: Marchers from the first demonstrations for homosexual rights, nurses of the AIDS years, performers of the night: across 250 portraits gathered at the National Portrait Gallery, Tim Walker ennobles the heralds of his community. L’article Tim Walker’s Queeristocracy Holds Court in…

blocks.caption: Paul O’Grady (1955–2023) and Julian Clary as the Glitter Queens, with Harry Browse, Rae and Liam Elias as the Glitter Boys, London, 2022, by Tim Walker © Tim Walker

blocks.text: Marchers from the first demonstrations for homosexual rights, nurses of the AIDS years, performers of the night: across 250 portraits gathered at the National Portrait Gallery, Tim Walker ennobles the heralds of his community.
By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Tim Walker.

blocks.caption: Aphra and Jo Barwick, Siobhan Fahey and Emily Witham, East Sussex, 2024, by Tim Walker © Tim Walker

blocks.text: Tim Walker came into the world on November 27, 1970, in England. That same day, on Highbury Fields, Britons marched for homosexual rights for the first time. Did this calendrical coincidence seal a destiny? Whatever the answer, the photographer took up with the queer community and its allies, and now exhibits 250 previously unseen portraits of them. “Fairyland is me saying you are not alone,” says Tim Walker.

blocks.caption: Francis Lee, Ode to Edward Carpenter, London, 2023, by Tim Walker © Tim Walker
Ben Whishaw in Crystal Prism, London, 2020, by Tim Walker © Tim Walker
Andrew Lumsden (1941–2023) (after Nicholas Hilliard), London, 2023, by Tim Walker © Tim Walker

blocks.text: Lace ruffs and gilded frames open the show: the trailblazers of the 1970s and 1980s pose in the finery of Tudor portraits painted by Hans Holbein the Younger, portraitist to Henry VIII, and Nicholas Hilliard, miniaturist to Elizabeth I. Tim Walker thus raises the founders of the Gay Liberation Front and Stonewall, Olivette Cole-Wilson and Lisa Power among them, into his own “queeristocracy.” Shona Heath, an Oscar winner for the sets of Poor Things , designed the exhibition. All of it unfolds along “a journey that begins with protest and outrage and ends with joy,” says curator Susanna Brown.

blocks.caption: Olivette Cole–Wilson and Blackbird, London, 2025, by Tim Walker © Tim Walker
Sunil Gupta, London, 2023, by Tim Walker © Tim Walker
Isaac Julien and Queen Conch Shell, London, 2023, by Tim Walker © Tim Walker

blocks.text: On the day of the shoot, each sitter arrives bearing a cherished object. Filmmaker Isaac Julien cradles a conch shell, a motif from his film Looking for Langston (1989); Welsh actress Jill Nalder, who inspired the character of Jill in It’s a Sin , holds in her open palm a photograph of actor Dursley McLinden, lost to AIDS in 1995. Writer Shon Faye, poet Kae Tempest and Lady Phyll, cofounder of UK Black Pride, pose against “deceivingly simple” white backgrounds inherited from Richard Avedon, the American master of the portrait whom Tim Walker assisted in the 1990s. Ian McKellen, for his part, spells the word Love with his fingers.

blocks.caption: Ian McKellen, Love, London, 2023, by Tim Walker © Tim Walker
Shon Faye, London, 2025, by Tim Walker © Tim Walker
Jill Nalder Holding a Photograph of Dursley McLinden (1965–95), London, 2023, by Tim Walker © Tim Walker

blocks.text: An entire room honors those who faced down the AIDS epidemic of the 1980s. Portraits of the nurses and doctors who developed effective treatments hang beside Marc Almond, voice of the synth-pop duo Soft Cell, Holly Johnson, singer of the Liverpool band Frankie Goes to Hollywood and Jimmy Somerville, whose falsetto carried Bronski Beat. “The brilliance of their music boomed despite the fear of mortality and discrimination. I wanted to bring that disco to the ward,” says Tim Walker. At the center, the Rebel Dykes, a lesbian collective out of post-punk London, pose on a grand scale, in the vein of the Zurich biker gangs photographed by Swiss photographer Karlheinz Weinberger.

blocks.caption: Kae Tempest, London, 2023, by Tim Walker © Tim Walker
Lady Phyll, London, 2024, by Tim Walker © Tim Walker
David Hoyle, Prawn Cocktailed, London, 2023, by Tim Walker © Tim Walker

blocks.text: Fashion, makeup and performance reign over the second half of the exhibition. French couturier Jean Paul Gaultier shares the walls with David Hoyle, a figure of English avant-garde cabaret, and Paul O’Grady, the comedian who died in 2023, unforgettable as Lily Savage, whom Tim Walker crowns a Glitter Queen beside comedian Julian Clary, amid clouds and bubbles. Victoria Siddall, director of the National Portrait Gallery, salutes these “lavish, fantastical scenes.” The last room gives way to the flesh, where eroticism reworks fairy tales and nursery rhymes. Tim Walker holds that voluptuousness, and the humor that rides with it, to be “the very heart of what we’re talking about when we talk about Queerness. A place where you can desire and be desired. A place where you can be whoever you want to be.”

blocks.caption: Fairyland Parade, Joe Sweeney, Matthew Keller, Harry Keita, Bolly Illusion, James Corbin, Oliver-Bijan Daryoush, Jack Newman, Yos Clark and Joseph O’Rourke, London, 2023, by Tim Walker © Tim Walker
Maartje Convens and Marin Céleste, Camfield Place, Hertfordshire, 2022, by Tim Walker © Tim Walker
Alex Gorey and Matías Montes (after Yannis Tsarouchis), London, 2021, by Tim Walker © Tim Walker

blocks.text: “Tim Walker’s Fairyland: Love and Legends” runs at the National Portrait Gallery, London, through February 7, 2027.
The exhibition catalogue, Tim Walker’s Fairyland: Love and Legends , is published by National Portrait Gallery Publications (320 pages, £35).
